note: This is not semantic Gold and no part of it is user-approved. It is a set of layout judgements about whether one reconstructed row holds one region or several, made by reading each row's text and glyph boxes.
It is kept apart from the segmentation rule on purpose. A rule that had these cases built into it would agree with them by construction, and the agreement would say nothing.
Every case names a document, a page and the row's Y, so it is re-derived from the source each run rather than stored as an outcome.

verdicts.DIVIDED: The row holds separate regions and the candidate must divide it.
verdicts.WHOLE: The row is one region and the candidate must leave it alone.
verdicts.UNDER_SPLIT: The row holds separate regions, the candidate leaves it whole, and that is recorded as a known miss rather than accepted as correct. Conservative: it costs a coarse atom, not a wrong one.

cases.reason: Issuing body on the left, national heading on the right. Two rows carry the same corridor, and both have text on either side of it.
The same masthead in English, over two rows: THE NATIONAL / ASSEMBLY against THE SOCIALIST REPUBLIC OF VIETNAM / Independence - Freedom - Happiness.
Document number on the left, place and date on the right, under a masthead row that divides at the same corridor.
As above, in a circular rather than a consolidated law.
Cells of an accounting table. The column corridors hold across the rows above and below.
Distribution list on the left, signing authority on the right. Two independent columns running down the closing page.
Gazette reference and page number. One region with a wide gap before the folio, and no neighbouring row keeps that gap open.
The same header with the folio on the other side. Still one region.

A watermark fragment lands on the baseline of a line of body text. It is arguably a separate region, but it appears at a different x on each row it touches, so there is no corridor to read. Left whole, and recorded as a residual rather than a success.

The same masthead as case 1, but this printing puts nothing to the left of the national heading on the second row, and the row above is a full-width running header. One row shows the division and no other confirms it, so the rule declines. The evidence really is one row; the cost is a coarse atom, not a wrong one.
